items.item: transaction_timestamp()/now() return the transaction's own start time and never change during that transaction
clock_timestamp() returns the actual current time and changes even within one statement, unlike transaction_timestamp()/now()

at.out: named as the contrasting function PostgreSQL itself documents; not independently exercised in this topic's own lab

items.item: a value handed out by nextval is not reclaimed for re-use if its own transaction later aborts

at.step: Reveal: sequence ids are not commit order either

items.item: An updated_at cursor's only real blind spot among the options a learner might guess is a hard delete, because a repeated read of an unchanged row is exactly what an idempotent merge is built to absorb harmlessly, measured directly across three repeats.

at.step: Predict: what a cursor can never see

items.item: A slow transaction's committed row is stamped with its own start time, not its commit time, so it can land behind a watermark a cursor already advanced past while that transaction was still open — measured directly: the cursor run found nothing while the transaction was open, advanced its watermark anyway, and the transaction's own later commit landed stamped behind that line.

A sequence-id cursor has the identical disagreement with commit order for a different reason: nextval hands out a value immediately and never reclaims it on rollback, so a transaction that grabbed an earlier number can still commit later than one that grabbed a later number.

at.step: Reveal: sequence ids are not commit order either

items.item: A lookback margin catches the missed row, and an idempotent merge keyed on the primary key makes re-reading that same row three times leave the row count and its data completely unchanged, measured directly.

at.step: Reveal: lookback plus idempotent merge, reproduced

items.item: The lookback margin has to be sized from the slowest transaction a source actually runs, measured, not assumed; a margin picked shorter than that recreates the exact miss it was meant to close.

A hard delete leaves no updated_at behind at all, measured directly: the source's own row count drops by one and a cursor query for that id after the deletion's own watermark finds nothing, which no lookback window, however wide, repairs.

at.step: Reveal: the one miss lookback cannot fix

items.item: A bulk UPDATE that writes every column except updated_at is mechanically identical to a hard delete from a cursor's point of view: the column is only ever set by whatever explicitly writes it, so skipping it leaves no timestamp signal that anything changed.

Once a source's transactions run long enough, or its intermediate states matter, a cursor built this way has outgrown what it can promise, and the fix becomes reading the source's own change log directly instead of polling a column after the fact — the decision rule this topic hands to 8.2.

Chapter 2 topic 9's MERGE/upsert atomicity and Chapter 3 topic 13's idempotent-merge-load pattern are the two prior-topic mechanisms this topic's own lookback fix reuses rather than re-teaches; Chapter 5 topic 11's isolation-anomaly vocabulary names the same commit-order-versus-timestamp-order disagreement this topic measures directly.
